articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1M tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The county commission extended its deal with Visit Pensacola last month with no public discussion. Records show the agency's overhead costs have doubled since 2022.
brief: Escambia County commissioners approved a $2.1 million contract extension with Visit Pensacola on April 17 without issuing a request for proposals or holding public discussion.

Administrative and overhead costs at the tourism marketing agency have grown from 18% to 37% of total expenditures since 2022, according to financial records obtained through a public records request.
Visit Pensacola CEO Darien Schaefer's compensation package now exceeds $285,000 annually, up from $198,000 three years ago.
articles.body:
The consent agenda moved fast on April 17. Seventeen items in under four minutes. No questions from the dais. No speakers at the podium. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh called for a vote and the gavel came down.

Buried on page 43 of the meeting packet was Item 14-C: a one-year extension of Escambia County's contract with Visit Pensacola, the nonprofit agency tasked with marketing the region to tourists. The price tag: $2.1 million in bed tax revenue.

The county commission approved the extension unanimously. There was no competitive bidding process. No public discussion. No mention of the agency's ballooning overhead costs or the CEO's 44% raise over three years.

"This is how it's always been done," said County Administrator Wes Moreno when reached by phone last week. "Visit Pensacola has been our tourism partner for over a decade. The relationship works."

Whether it works—and for whom—depends on which numbers you examine.

The money trail

Visit Pensacola operates as a 501(c)(6) nonprofit under contract with Escambia County. Its funding comes from the county's Tourist Development Tax, a 5% levy on short-term rentals and hotel rooms. The agency received $1.8 million in fiscal year 2022, $1.95 million in 2023, and $2.1 million in the current contract period.

Financial records obtained through a public records request show where that money goes—and how the allocation has shifted.

In fiscal year 2022, Visit Pensacola reported spending 82% of its budget on marketing, advertising and destination promotion. Administrative costs, including salaries, benefits, office expenses and professional services, consumed the remaining 18%.

By fiscal year 2025, those proportions had changed dramatically. Marketing expenditures dropped to 63% of the budget. Administrative and overhead costs climbed to 37%—more than double the 2022 rate.

The agency's most recent IRS Form 990, covering calendar year 2024, shows CEO Darien Schaefer received total compensation of $285,412. That figure includes a base salary of $218,000, a $35,000 performance bonus, and $32,412 in benefits and retirement contributions.

In 2022, Schaefer's total compensation was $198,650.

"Executive compensation is set by our board of directors based on market comparisons and performance metrics," Schaefer said in an emailed statement. "Visit Pensacola consistently delivers strong results for Escambia County's tourism economy."

The agency declined to make Schaefer available for an interview.

No alternatives considered

Florida law does not require counties to competitively bid contracts with nonprofit tourism agencies. But it doesn't prohibit it either.

Escambia County's purchasing policy, updated in 2019, states that professional services contracts exceeding $500,000 "should be subject to a competitive selection process unless the Board of County Commissioners determines that a sole-source arrangement serves the public interest."

No such determination appears in the April 17 meeting minutes or the contract extension itself. The agenda item simply describes the extension as "renewal of existing agreement."

Commissioner Steven Barry, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he was comfortable with the arrangement.

"Visit Pensacola knows this market," Barry said. "Starting over with a new vendor would mean a learning curve. That costs money too."

Asked whether the commission had reviewed the agency's overhead costs before voting, Barry said he had not examined the detailed financials. "I trust our staff to flag any concerns," he said.

Commissioner Bergosh did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Tourism numbers and context

Visit Pensacola points to tourism metrics as evidence of its effectiveness. The agency's 2024 annual report claims 6.2 million visitors to Escambia County, generating $3.8 billion in economic impact.

Those figures come from Tourism Economics, a consulting firm hired by Visit Pensacola to produce the estimates. The methodology relies on modeling and extrapolation rather than direct measurement.

Bed tax collections—a more concrete indicator—tell a more complicated story. Revenue peaked at $14.2 million in fiscal year 2023, dropped to $13.1 million in 2024, and is projected at $12.8 million for the current fiscal year.

Visit Pensacola attributes the decline to increased competition from other Gulf Coast destinations and a broader pullback in discretionary travel spending.

"Headwinds exist in every tourism market right now," Schaefer's statement said. "Our job is to ensure Pensacola remains competitive. The alternative—cutting marketing—would accelerate the decline."

What other counties do

Escambia's arrangement is not unusual for Florida. Many counties contract with nonprofit destination marketing organizations using bed tax revenue, and many do so without competitive bidding.

But some have moved in a different direction.

Hillsborough County issued an RFP for its tourism marketing contract in 2023, ultimately awarding the work to Visit Tampa Bay after reviewing three proposals. Bay County conducted a similar process in 2022.

"Competition keeps everyone sharp," said Dr. Kelly Semrad, a hospitality professor at the University of Central Florida who studies destination marketing. "It forces agencies to justify their overhead and demonstrate value. Without that pressure, costs tend to drift upward."

Santa Rosa County, which shares Pensacola Beach with Escambia, takes a different approach entirely. The county handles tourism marketing in-house through its economic development office, spending roughly $800,000 annually—less than half of Visit Pensacola's contract.

Santa Rosa's bed tax collections have grown 12% over the past three years. Escambia's have declined 10%.

What happens next

The current contract runs through September 30, 2027. Under its terms, either party may terminate with 180 days notice.

The agreement requires Visit Pensacola to submit quarterly financial reports to the county's Tourist Development Council, an advisory board composed of hotel operators, vacation rental owners and tourism industry representatives. The TDC reviews those reports but has no authority to modify or reject them.

County Commissioner Lumon May, who represents District 3, said he plans to request a detailed briefing on Visit Pensacola's finances before the next contract renewal comes up.

"Two million dollars is real money," May said. "The public deserves to know exactly where it goes. I'd like to see those numbers broken down in a public meeting, not just buried in a consent agenda."

Whether that review will include consideration of competitive bidding remains unclear.

"I'm not saying we need to make a change," May said. "I'm saying we need to ask the questions."

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's empty storefronts: A block-by-block count
articles.dek: Palafox Street looks busy on weekend nights. But a Flightline survey found 23 ground-floor vacancies between Main and Government—more than double the count from three years ago.
brief: A Flightline survey counted 23 ground-floor vacancies on Palafox Street between Main and Government streets, up from 11 in 2023
The 100 block of South Palafox has the highest concentration with seven empty storefronts, including three former restaurants
Commercial rents on Palafox have risen 34% since 2021 while foot traffic remains below pre-pandemic levels according to Downtown Improvement Board data
articles.body:
The paper signs went up in the windows of Bodacious Bookshop on a Tuesday in March. By Friday, the shelves were empty. By the following week, the only evidence the store had existed for 14 years was a sun-faded rectangle on the brick where the hanging sign used to be.

Walk that stretch of South Palafox today and you'll pass the blank storefront on your way to six others just like it.

The Flightline spent three days in late April surveying every ground-floor commercial space on Palafox Street between Main Street and Government Street—the six-block corridor that serves as downtown Pensacola's retail and dining spine. We counted storefronts, documented vacancies, photographed window signage and contacted property owners where possible.

The count: 23 empty storefronts out of 87 total ground-floor commercial spaces. That's a 26.4% vacancy rate.

In May 2023, using the same methodology, The Flightline counted 11 vacancies along the same stretch—a 12.6% rate.

Block by block

The damage isn't distributed evenly.

The 100 block of South Palafox, running from Garden Street to Main Street, has the highest concentration of vacancies. Seven of 16 storefronts sit empty. Three of those formerly housed restaurants: the spaces that held Angelena's, a casual Italian spot that closed in January; the former Wild Greg's Saloon location, dark since October; and a corner unit that has cycled through two concepts since 2024 without either lasting more than eight months.

The 0 block—technically North Palafox, between Garden and Government—fares better. Three vacancies among 14 storefronts. But two of those are large anchor spaces: the former home of a regional bank branch and a two-story retail building that hasn't had a tenant since a furniture store departed in late 2024.

The 100 and 200 blocks of South Palafox, the stretch closest to the waterfront and Palafox Pier, show the most resilience. Combined vacancy rate: 18%. But even here, longtime tenants have departed. A gift shop that operated for two decades is now a "Coming Soon" sign for a concept that property records show was announced 11 months ago.

The rent question

Ask downtown business owners why storefronts sit empty and you'll hear one word more than any other: rent.

"I signed my lease in 2019 at $22 a square foot," said Marcus Webb, who operates a men's clothing store on the 100 block. "My renewal offer last fall was $34. I took it because where else am I going to go? But the sandwich shop next door didn't. They're gone."

Data from the Downtown Improvement Board, obtained through a public records request, shows average asking rents for ground-floor Palafox retail space have risen from $19.50 per square foot in 2021 to $26.15 in the board's most recent quarterly survey. That's a 34% increase.

The same data shows that monthly foot traffic counts at four sensor locations along Palafox have not returned to 2019 levels. The March 2026 count was 12% below March 2019.

"The math just doesn't work for a lot of operators," said Diane Schultz, a commercial real estate broker with Realty Masters who has handled downtown leases for 15 years. "Rents went up because property values went up, because interest rates went up, because insurance went up. But the customer base didn't grow to match."

Who owns empty downtown

Property records reveal a concentrated ownership pattern among the vacant storefronts.

Three LLCs controlled by local developer Ray Russenberger own buildings containing six of the 23 vacancies. Russenberger did not respond to two phone calls and an email requesting comment.

An Atlanta-based investment group, Southeastern Retail Partners, owns two buildings with a combined four vacancies. A representative said the company is "actively marketing" the spaces but declined to discuss asking rents or leasing terms.

Five vacancies are in buildings owned by estate trusts or out-of-state individuals who could not be reached.

The remaining eight are distributed among local property owners, several of whom said they have turned down prospective tenants.

"I had a vape shop offer me above asking," said Helen Kendrick, who owns a building on the 0 block with one vacant storefront. "I said no. I had a check cashing place. Said no. I'd rather wait for the right fit than hurt what's left of this street."

What fills the gaps

Not every storefront that empties stays empty. The Flightline documented 12 new tenants that have opened on the surveyed blocks since May 2023. But the pattern is notable.

Seven of the 12 are service businesses rather than retail: a law office, an insurance agency, a therapy practice, a co-working space, two salons and a tattoo parlor. These operations typically generate less foot traffic than retail stores and often keep limited public hours.

Three are restaurants or bars, though one of those—a cocktail lounge in a former retail space—opened just six weeks ago.

Two are retail: a vintage clothing shop and a store selling crystals and spiritual goods.

"The retail-to-service shift is real and it's accelerating," said Dr. Janet Morrison, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies regional commercial trends. "It's not unique to Pensacola. But it does change the character of a downtown when you walk past law offices instead of shop windows."

City Hall's view

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves, asked about the vacancy rate during a press availability last week, pointed to planned infrastructure improvements.

"We're investing $3.2 million in streetscape upgrades on Palafox this year," Reeves said. "New lighting, new sidewalks, more greenery. That makes downtown more attractive to businesses and visitors both."

Pressed on whether the city has tools to address rising commercial rents, Reeves said market forces were largely beyond municipal control.

"We can make downtown a great place to do business. We can't tell property owners what to charge."

Escambia County Commissioner Lumon May, whose district includes downtown, has floated the idea of a commercial vacancy tax—a fee assessed on property owners who leave storefronts empty beyond a certain period. Such measures exist in a handful of cities including San Francisco and Washington, D.C.

"If you're sitting on an empty building waiting for rents to go even higher, that hurts the whole downtown," May said in an interview. "There ought to be some cost to that."

The proposal has not been formally introduced. County staff said they are researching legal questions around implementation.

Summer test

Memorial Day weekend will mark the unofficial start of downtown Pensacola's tourism season. Hotel bookings are strong, according to Visit Pensacola. Palafox will fill with visitors.

Many of them will walk past blank windows.

"People come here expecting something," said Webb, the clothing store owner. "They saw pictures online, they heard it was a cool downtown. Then they get here and half the storefronts are dark. That's the reputation we're building."

At Bodacious Bookshop's former location, the paper in the windows has started to yellow. A small tear in one corner lets passersby glimpse the empty shelves inside.

No "For Lease" sign has appeared. The property owner, an LLC registered to a Pensacola address, has not returned calls.

The storefront, like 22 others on this stretch, waits.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's new gate system has cut wait times. Neighbors say it pushed traffic onto their streets.
articles.dek: The base installed automated lanes in March to speed up morning entry. Residents on Navy Boulevard say the backups just moved a half-mile west.
brief: NAS Pensacola's automated gate lanes have reduced base entry wait times by 40%, according to Navy officials.
Residents on Navy Boulevard and adjacent streets report traffic backups now begin forming at 5:45 a.m., a half-mile from the main gate.
Escambia County is studying signal timing changes but says any major fixes would require coordination with the Navy.
articles.body:
At 6:15 on a Tuesday morning, Linda Carver stood at the end of her driveway on Fairfield Drive and counted cars. Thirty-seven in the first five minutes. Most were heading east toward NAS Pensacola's main gate, creeping past her mailbox at walking speed.

"Before March, I could back out of my driveway at 6:30 and be fine," Carver said. "Now I have to wait for a gap. Some mornings I just give up and go back inside."

The change Carver noticed coincides with NAS Pensacola's installation of three automated entry lanes at the main gate. The system, which went live March 3, uses RFID readers to scan Department of Defense identification cards without requiring drivers to stop and hand credentials to a guard.

Navy officials say the upgrade has been a success. Wait times during the morning rush have dropped from an average of 22 minutes to 13 minutes, according to data provided by NAS Pensacola's public affairs office. The base processes roughly 8,500 vehicles through the main gate on a typical weekday.

"The automated lanes have significantly improved throughput while maintaining our security standards," said Lt. Cmdr. Marcus Webb, the base's public affairs officer. "We're pleased with the results."

But residents who live along Navy Boulevard and the residential streets that feed into it say the math doesn't add up. If cars are getting through the gate faster, they ask, why are the backups worse than ever?

The bottleneck moved

The answer, according to several residents and one traffic engineer who reviewed the situation, is that the new system created a new problem. The automated lanes can process cars faster than the old manual checkpoints. But the security screening area just inside the gate—where randomly selected vehicles are pulled aside for inspection—hasn't changed.

The result: cars now queue on Navy Boulevard waiting to enter the pre-screening zone instead of waiting at the gate itself.

"You moved the bottleneck," said Ron Atchison, a retired civil engineer who lives on West Navy Boulevard. "The gate can handle more cars per hour. But the chokepoint is still there. It's just 800 feet closer to my house now."

Atchison has been tracking traffic patterns since April. He provided The Flightline with a spreadsheet showing vehicle counts at the intersection of Navy Boulevard and Fairfield Drive. On 14 of the 18 weekday mornings he measured, traffic began backing up past his street by 5:50 a.m.—roughly 40 minutes earlier than the backups typically reached that point before the gate upgrade.

NAS Pensacola officials did not dispute Atchison's observations but said the base's responsibility ends at its perimeter.

"Traffic flow on Navy Boulevard is under the jurisdiction of Escambia County," Lt. Cmdr. Webb said in an email. "We coordinate with local authorities when requested, but road infrastructure outside the installation is not within our purview."

County caught in the middle

Escambia County Public Works Director Janet Simmons said her department has received 23 complaints about Navy Boulevard traffic since March. The county is studying whether adjustments to signal timing at three intersections could help, but she cautioned that options are limited.

"Navy Boulevard is a state road," Simmons said. "We maintain it under an agreement with FDOT, but any significant changes—adding turn lanes, modifying access points—would require state approval and state funding."

The Florida Department of Transportation said it has not received a formal request from the county regarding Navy Boulevard but would review any proposal submitted through standard channels.

Simmons said the county has reached out to NAS Pensacola to discuss coordinated solutions, including the possibility of staggering shift start times to spread out the morning rush. Those conversations are ongoing, she said, but no agreements have been reached.

"The Navy has been responsive," Simmons said. "But this is a complicated situation with a lot of stakeholders."

'We're not anti-Navy'

On a Saturday afternoon, about two dozen residents gathered at Marcus Pointe Baptist Church for an informal meeting organized by Carver and several neighbors. The mood was frustrated but measured.

"We're not anti-Navy," said Thomas Perkins, who has lived on West Navy Boulevard for 31 years. "Half the people in this room are veterans or have family on that base. But someone needs to think about what happens when you make changes that affect people off the installation."

Several attendees said they had contacted Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes the area. Bergosh did not respond to requests for comment from The Flightline.

Carver said she plans to attend the next county commission meeting to request a formal traffic study. She's also started a petition asking NAS Pensacola to evaluate the impact of the new gate system on surrounding neighborhoods.

"They're measuring success by how fast people get on base," Carver said. "Nobody's measuring what's happening to the people who live here."

Back on Fairfield Drive, Carver has adjusted her schedule. She now leaves for her job at Sacred Heart Hospital by 5:30 a.m., a full hour earlier than before March.

"I'm not fighting it anymore," she said. "I just get up earlier. But that's not a solution. That's me giving up."
